Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

newspaper noun

also newspapers, the papers, daily paper, gazette

classical

Tac. A. 13.31: diurnīs urbis āctīs
Suet. Jul. 20: ut tam senātūs quam populī diurna ācta cōnfierent et pūblicārentur (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 351
Levi–Bini p. 30

ācta diurna, āctōrum diurnōrum n. pl.

the daily gazette; a newspaper

The daily record of the senate and the people that Caesar had published (Suet. Jul. 20): the Roman newspaper, read in the provinces and the armies (Tac. A. 16.22). Also diurna alone, or diurna āctōrum scrīptūra (Tac. A. 3.3). A weekly is ācta hebdomadālia (Traupman 351).

Other words

  • diārium, diāriī n. — a newspaper

    noun, second declension · also used · modern · Traupman 351, 405

    Classically a day’s ration, and once a diary (Lewis & Short). A morning paper, diārium mātūtīnum; an evening paper, diārium vespertīnum (Traupman 351).

  • ephēmeris, ephēmeridis f. — a newspaper; any periodical

    noun, third declension · also used · modern · M-O s.v. magazine: newspaper; Levi–Bini p. 30

    Classically a day-book or diary (Cic. Quinct. 57, Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • diurna populī Rōmānī per prōvinciās, per exercitūs cūrātius leguntur, ut nōscātur quid Thrasea nōn fēcerit.

    The daily gazette of the Roman people is read with special care in the provinces and the armies, to find out what Thrasea has not done.Tac. A. 16.22

  • cum ex dignitāte populī Rōmānī repertum sit rēs inlūstrīs annālibus, tālia diurnīs urbis āctīs mandāre

    since it has been found fitting for the dignity of the Roman people to leave great events to history, and such things to the city’s daily gazetteTac. A. 13.31

See also article, magazine, media, read.
